title: How to protect your savings from inflation using low-risk asset classes
description: A deeper look at TIPS, I-Bonds, and Floating Rate Notes.
content:
Inflation is the invisible tax on cash. If you hold $100,000 in a checking account during 5% inflation, you lose $5,000 of purchasing power in a year. You didn't spend it; it just evaporated. To defend your wealth, you cannot stay in nominal cash. You must move to 'Real Assets' or financial instruments explicitly designed to track the Consumer Price Index (CPI). This guide focuses on the safest tier of inflation protection—government-backed securities that guarantee your money keeps up with the cost of living.

Key Takeaways

  • I-Bonds are the Ultimate Shield: Series I Savings Bonds have a composite rate that adjusts every 6 months based on inflation. They cannot lose value nominally.
  • TIPS (Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities): Bonds where the *principal* value increases with inflation. Best used in tax-advantaged accounts due to 'phantom income' tax.
  • Floating Rate Notes (FRNs): US Treasury notes where the interest rate resets weekly. If the Fed raises rates to fight inflation, your payout rises instantly.
  • Avoid Long Duration: During inflation, interest rates usually rise, crashing the price of long-term bonds. Stick to short-term assets to preserve capital.

Why It Matters (US Context)

The US Treasury creates specific products to help citizens fight inflation. However, I-Bonds have a purchase limit ($10k/year) and TIPS have complex tax rules. Navigating these constraints is key to building a localized inflation hedge.

The Inflation-Linked Menu

Choose the tool based on your liquidity needs.

1. Series I Savings Bonds

  • Mechanism: Fixed Rate + Inflation Rate. If inflation is high, yield is high.
  • Limit: $10,000 per SSN per calendar year.
  • Liquidity: Locked for 1 year. 3-month interest penalty if sold < 5 years.
  • Verdict: The best 'Emergency Fund' extension for long-term cash.

2. TIPS (Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities)

  • Mechanism: If inflation is 3%, the face value of your $1,000 bond becomes $1,030. You get interest on the higher amount.
  • Tax Trap: You owe IRS taxes on the $30 'phantom' growth even though you didn't receive the cash yet.
  • Verdict: Hold in an IRA to avoid the tax headache.

3. Short-Term T-Bills

While not explicitly inflation-linked, short-term bills (3-month) allow you to constantly reinvest at higher rates as the Fed hikes rates to fight inflation. They act as a natural hedge without the complexity of TIPS.

Portfolio Construction

  1. The 'Core' Hedge: Max out I-Bonds ($10k) every January if you have excess cash. Over 5 years, you build a $50k inflation-proof tiered emergency fund.
  2. The 'Taxable' Hedge: In your brokerage, use USFR (Floating Rate Treasury ETF). It holds ultra-short government debt. It yields ~5% when rates are high and has almost zero price volatility.
  3. The 'Real' Hedge: Stocks and Real Estate. Over 20 years, companies raise prices to match inflation. Equities are the best long-term hedge; I-Bonds are the best short-term hedge.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Gold better?

Gold is volatile. In 2022, inflation hit 9% and Gold dropped. It is an unreliable hedge. I-Bonds are mathematically linked to CPI, offering a guaranteed match.

Can I buy I-Bonds in an IRA?

No. You must buy them at TreasuryDirect.gov. They live outside your brokerage accounts.

What if deflation happens?

TIPS can lose principal value (down to par) in deflation. I-Bonds cannot go below 0%. I-Bonds have a 'deflation floor', making them safer.
